shots.act: ACT I · THE NIGHT THE ATLANTIC WENT SILENT
shots.narration: At 8:32 PM Universal Time on November 18, 1929, six transatlantic telegraph cables south of Newfoundland went dead at the exact same instant. An undersea earthquake had just struck.

shots.narration: In 1929, the seabed off Newfoundland was the busiest cable crossroads on Earth—linking North American stock markets and newsrooms directly to Europe.

shots.narration: Automatic recorders stamped the exact minute any circuit failed. On shore, a Wheatstone bridge measured the surviving copper's electrical resistance—converting ohms straight into nautical miles to the break.

shots.narration: At sea, repair ships worked nearly a year grappling severed lines from three miles down. When hydrographer Vladimir de Smitt mapped all twenty-eight breaks across twelve cables, an extraordinary pattern emerged.

shots.act: ACT IV · TWENTY-THREE YEARS OF WRONG ANSWERS
shots.narration: Why would steel cables break half a day after an earthquake stopped? In Nature, geologist J. W. Gregory blamed parallel faults unzipping southward. Yet seismographs recorded only two aftershocks—both back at the original epicenter.

shots.narration: Today, that discovery protects the digital world. Over 1.8 million kilometers of garden-hose-thin fiber-optic cables cross the seafloor, carrying more than ninety-nine percent of intercontinental internet traffic.

shots.act: ACT VII · THE FRAGILE FLOOR OF THE INTERNET
shots.narration: Once again, cables clocked the surge: Tonga's domestic line snapped at 4:30 AM, and its international fiber broke seventy-four minutes later—wrecking 194 kilometers of cable and isolating a nation for five weeks.
